kakekotoba.interaction: 秋 (autumn) is homophonous with 飽き (weariness/being tired of a lover/life). The surface statement 'it is not autumn for me alone' also carries the undertone 'it is not that I alone am weary/forsaken,' linking the seasonal universality of autumn's melancholy to a suggestion of personal romantic disappointment shared by all. This is the classical double reading exploited throughout the Kokinshū for 秋/飽き.

bipartite.kami_theme: Gazing at the moon, the speaker feels a diffuse, thousand-fold sorrow welling up without clear cause.
bipartite.shimo_theme: The speaker checks and qualifies this feeling: the autumn (and its sadness) is not his alone — it is universal, shared by all who view the moon.
bipartite.pivot_note: The kami-no-ku presents an intense, almost solipsistic personal sorrow triggered by moon-viewing ('a thousand-fold sadness'), while the shimo-no-ku pulls back from that solipsism with a reflective, almost philosophical correction — asserting that autumn's melancholy belongs to everyone, not the speaker uniquely. The pivot is the move from raw subjective feeling to universalizing self-awareness, turning private grief into a meditation on the shared human condition under the autumn moon.

kigo.note: 月 (tsuki, the moon) here specifically evokes the autumn moon (aki no tsuki), the most celebrated moon-viewing season in the classical canon, associated with heightened clarity of light and with melancholy reflection. Its pairing with 秋 in ku 5 confirms this is the autumn moon of moon-viewing (tsukimi) tradition, the central seasonal image of the poem, dominant over the merely conceptual 秋 in the final line, which functions as gloss/pivot rather than independent image.

source_jp:
月見れば
千々に物こそ
悲しけれ
わが身ひとつの
秋にはあらねど
